title: Twentieth Century

evidence.note: Columbia Pictures release; general release 11 May 1934 (premiere at Radio City Music Hall on 3 May 1934), per the Wikipedia film article. Renewal search: our script flagged six renewal hits that name other titles (After Tonight, As the Earth Turns, Bosko in Dutch, The Bowery, Broadway Knights, The Cat and the Fiddle). 'Twentieth Century' appears in them only as a claimant name (Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. or 20th Century Pictures). The record of which volume and year the script searched was not kept, and I did not re-read the volumes or the flagged entries. I also did not run a full-text search of the 1961 and 1962 renewal volumes (Catalog of Copyright Entries, Motion Pictures) or the Copyright Office catalog. No renewal search has been completed, so renewal and non-renewal are both unconfirmed.

Inference, not evidence. This is a sound film. A soundtrack recorded for a film normally shares the film's copyright status, and the film's status is unresolved. No source was checked for the soundtrack itself.

Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur adapted their 1932 Broadway play Twentieth Century, which was itself based on Charles Bruce Millholland's unproduced play Napoleon of Broadway. The copyright and renewal status of the play was not checked.

editorial:
Twentieth Century is Howard Hawks's 1934 screwball comedy for Columbia Pictures. A flamboyant Broadway producer (John Barrymore) tries to win back the star he created (Carole Lombard), mostly on a train. Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur adapted their own 1932 Broadway play, which drew on Charles Bruce Millholland's unproduced play Napoleon of Broadway. The film was released 11 May 1934, runs about 91 minutes, and was selected for the National Film Registry in December 2011 (per the Wikipedia article). A creator would want it for the Barrymore and Lombard performances and the train setting.

The rights trap is that the print's status is unresolved. No renewal search has been completed for this film, so this dossier does not claim the print is free or that it was left unrenewed. The only hits our script flagged were six other titles where 'Twentieth Century' appears as a claimant name; those entries were not re-read. Even if the film's renewal is absent, the underlying 1932 play is a separate copyright with its own renewal question. Check the Copyright Office records and the play's registration before relying on any copy.
faq: Is Twentieth Century (1934) public domain in the US?

Not confirmed. The film came out in 1934, so it is free only if its notice was missing or its renewal in 1961 or 1962 was never filed. No renewal search has been completed: the only hits our script flagged were six other titles where 'Twentieth Century' appears as a claimant name, and those were not re-read. Run the Copyright Office and Catalog of Copyright Entries searches linked above before reuse.
Can I use a copy found online, such as on the Internet Archive?

A copy being online says nothing about the film's copyright, and we did not verify any specific upload. Confirm the print's status first. Also check the underlying 1932 Hecht and MacArthur play, which has its own term and renewal history.
